The physical terminal allocation is valid in every permitted orientationThe first point is that a positive U really supplies the two terminal occurrences used in  $t_\tau$ .In canonical positive alignment,  $U(b,d,e)$  has terminals
$$(d,1),\qquad (e,b).$$
Their physical tiles are
$$\{d,d+1\}\times\{0,1\},
\qquad
\{e,e+1\}\times\{b,b+1\}.$$
The first contains precisely the original terminal endpoint and its two original supports
$$(d,0),\qquad(d+1,1);$$
the second contains the corresponding endpoint and supports
$$(e,b+1),\qquad(e+1,b).$$
The even depths ensure the stated tile alignment. The depth lower bound keeps these tiles away from the bar, and  $b\ge6$  makes the two terminal tiles distinct. Unequal depths cause no problem. The established charge-phase catalogue and tile-preserving symmetries transport this description to every positive U orientation.Consequently,
$$\sum_\tau t_\tau=2P(Y)$$
counts exactly two labelled terminal occurrences per added positive source.There is also a useful pointwise restriction:
$$t_\tau\le n_\tau(K).$$
Every terminal occurrence contributes an endpoint in that tile, and distinct occurrences have distinct endpoints. Therefore an actual negative singleton tile owned by a new positive U has exactly one new terminal occurrence. A negative singleton owned by an old U or by a rotor has none.This resolves the possible multiplicity concern. Several terminal credits can land in one physical tile after activation, but they remain separate allocations from distinct source occurrences. They cannot produce multiple terminal credits in a final singleton tile.The anchor allocation is equally well defined. Each new positive source contributes one unit at one chosen endpoint tile. Several sources may choose the same physical tile;  $p_Q$  correctly counts sources, rather than distinct anchor tiles.2.
